name: Codex Argenteus
material: Purple-dyed vellum, silver and gold ink
maker: Scribe working in the tradition of Wulfila's Bible
description: The Silver Bible, a sixth-century manuscript of Wulfila's Gothic Bible translation written in silver and gold ink on purple-dyed vellum, probably copied in northern Italy for the Ostrogothic court. Rediscovered at the monastery of Werden, it came to Sweden during the Thirty Years' War and is now kept at Uppsala University Library. It is the most substantial surviving text in the Gothic language. The manuscript is written in silver uncial script on leaves stained with purple dye, a colour reserved for imperial books, and only the gospel canon tables and a few headings are picked out in gold. Of its original two hundred or so leaves about 188 survive, making it the longest witness to the Gothic tongue, which was spoken by the East Germanic peoples into the Middle Ages. The codex has been studied, repaired, and reproduced again and again since its arrival in Sweden, and it remains a treasure of European cultural history.

name: The Church Bell Against Storms
powers: Its ringing breaks up storms, drives away evil, and helps stop fires.
description: Swedish church bells were believed to protect the parish: they were rung to break up thunderclouds, drive away storms and pestilence, and even to help stop fires. The casting of a new bell was accompanied by rites, and the bells were thought to carry a blessing that evil powers could not withstand. Ringing against bad weather ('ringning mot oväder') is recorded in many Swedish parishes. The sound of the consecrated bell was held to drive off the trolls and evil spirits that raised the weather, and the clergy were asked to ring while a storm passed, sometimes with a formula of words recited as the bell swung. When a fire broke out, the same bell was rung to alarm the parish and, in folk belief, to check the flames themselves. The rite of casting — pouring the bronze with prayers and watching over the new bell — made each bell a sacred object, and church bells were consequently treated with the respect owed to relics.
source: Swedish parish tradition of bell ringing against the weather

name: The Cat of Norrhult
description: A bewitched cat in a folk tale from Norrhult in Småland. In the tale 'The Cat of Norrhult', a cat behaves in ways that betray a witch's or troll's power behind it, and the cat's strange actions reveal the magic at work in the village. Cats were the favourite disguise of witches and of the trolls' servants in Nordic belief, and a cat that walked on two legs, spoke, or wore something out of place was read as the true witch showing herself. The tale belongs to the wide Swedish family of stories about animals that are not what they seem, where the sharp eye of a neighbour or the luck of a household exposes the creature. In Norrhult the cat gives the village its name for the wonder, and the story still colours how the place remembers the event.

name: The Cowbell of the Skogsrå
maker: Worn or carried by the forest spirit
powers: Its tinkling warns of the skogsrå's presence in the woods.
description: A cowbell heard in the forest in Swedish belief, and a mark of the skogsrå, the forest spirit who leads cattle astray. She is said to ring her bell or to ride a cow, and the tinkle of a bell where no cow is to be seen warns the woodsman or the herder of her presence. The cowbell ties the skogsrå to her trade of seducing cattle into the forest, where she keeps them in her care and returns them only on her own terms; a herd that wandered off was said to be 'with the skogsrå'. Her bell is a sound of both warning and temptation, for she appears as a beautiful woman from behind and a hollow or tailed thing when seen clearly. The cowbell is part of the skogsrå's folklore as a seductive and misleading spirit, whose call the wary were meant to resist.

name: The Church Keys
material: Iron or brass key and a Bible
maker: Church key, used by the household
powers: Turns or shakes to reveal the name of a thief.
description: The church key used in the Swedish divination called nyckelprövning, the key test. A key was bound between the pages of a Bible, which was then hung or turned while names were read, and it was believed the key would point out or shake at the name of a thief. The key-and-Bible test is documented in Swedish folk tradition for finding stolen goods, and it was trusted because the church key and the holy book brought God's judgement into the search. The test belonged to the wider family of divination by the Bible, psalm, or sieve that country people used when the law could not find the guilty. Because the outcome could ruin a name, the practice was discouraged by the clergy, yet it lingered in villages into the 19th century as a feared and resorted-to last judgement.
source: Swedish folk tradition of the key-and-Bible test

name: Kirkebåt (Church Boat)
description: A long rowing boat shared by a whole parish to carry people to Sunday service, built clinker of pine or oak and owned jointly by several farms. Church boats rowed people across fjords and lakes until the early 1900s, carrying fifty or more parishioners at a time; surviving examples like the Rols from Stryn are kept and rowed again. Racing between parishes on the way home was part of the tradition. The kirkebåt was a true communal vessel, each farm holding a share and supplying rowers, and the boat itself served as the village's gathering place on the water as the crew sang and traded news on the long pull to church. When roads reached the fjord settlements the great boats were laid up, but many were preserved, and the old race-rowing has been revived as a summer sport along the Norwegian coast.

name: Cauldron of the Underjordiske
powers: Lent by the mound folk, who always return what they borrow.
description: In Danish legend the underjordiske, the folk who live inside burial mounds and under the fields, are said to borrow pots, kettles, and spoons from farmhouses, as when a mound-man calls, lend me kettle and spoon, while I cook lamb soup under the hill. They always return what they borrow, and those who refused their request brought misfortune on the household. The motif is recorded in Evald Tang Kristensen's great collections of Jutland legends. The borrowed cauldron is a reminder that the hidden folk and the farmers shared a domestic world of borrowed pots and bargains kept.

name: Caduceus
powers: Charm of the herald; conduces the souls of the dead to the underworld; later sign of peace and commerce.
description: Hermes' herald's staff, first described as a rod wrapped with fillets or ribbons and only later twined with serpents; it charmed mortals and spirits and led the souls of the dead to the underworld. In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the god trades it for his newly invented lyre, and in later art it appears winged and entwined with two snakes. Through the Romans it became the sign of peace, commerce, and the herald's craft, and it survives today as a symbol of commerce and of the medical profession, though the rod of Asclepius is the older emblem of healing.
source: Homeric Hymn to Hermes; later literary and artistic tradition

name: Arrows of Cupid
powers: The golden arrow kindles love; the blunt leaden one drives love away.
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses are of two kinds: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away, and the pair together explain the passions of gods and mortals alike. When Apollo taunts Cupid about his bow, the boy shoots the golden arrow into Apollo and the leaden into the nymph Daphne, so that the god burns with desire while she flees him in terror, and the chase ends only when Daphne is changed into the laurel tree. The two arrows turn love and rejection into a kind of physics of the heart, a divine mechanism behind human obsession and coldness alike. The imagery was taken up endlessly in Renaissance and Baroque art, where a gold-tipped and a lead-tipped shaft dangle from Cupid's quiver. The motif survives in the everyday phrase 'arrows of love' and in Cupid's double quiver as the emblem of love's cruelty and arbitrariness.

name: Corona Civica
material: Oak leaves (holm, esculent, or common oak)
powers: Rewarded a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; granted lifelong honour and the right to sit with senators.
description: The corona civica, the civic crown of oak leaves, was Rome's highest honour for a citizen soldier, awarded to the man who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground where he did it; Pliny the Elder in the Natural History and Aulus Gellius in the Attic Nights describe its rules. Woven from holm, esculent, or common oak, it was granted by the rescued man himself, who was bound to honour his saviour as a parent, and the crown carried with it the right to wear it for life, to sit with the senators at the games, and to be free of many burdens; its inscription 'ob cives servatos', 'for saving citizens', became the slogan of imperial beneficence. Pliny records that it was counted second only to the grass crown, the corona obsidionalis, in the scale of Roman decorations, and Julius Caesar and later emperors displayed it with pride. The oak crown remained a political symbol of protection down to the end of the empire.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Book 16); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights (Book 5)

name: Chest of El Cid
powers: A ruse: sand offered as treasure to raise funds from the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas.
description: The chest of El Cid is the wooden coffer, bound with iron, that the exiled hero in the Cantar de Mio Cid fills with sand and pawns to the moneylenders Raquel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of gold, to raise the funds his banishment has denied him. The poem has El Cid swear the chest is full of pure gold, and the lenders accept it on his word, never daring to open it, and the ruse lets the hero mock the greed of the Jews while financing his campaign; the joke is that the treasure is worthless sand and the bargain is never meant to be redeemed. The episode, told with wry comedy, is one of the most famous of the epic, showing the hero's resourcefulness and his contempt for those who trust appearances. It is a literary invention with no historical basis, and no such chest is known to have existed. The chest remains a stock image of the confidence trick that passes off worthlessness as wealth.

name: Caladbolg
powers: Legendary sword of Cú Chulainn, capable of slicing the head off a boar with a single stroke.
description: Caladbolg, the great sword of Irish legend, is carried in the Ulster Cycle by Fergus mac Róich, the strong-armed former king of Ulster, and in some traditions it is also the blade of Cú Chulainn, who is said to have wielded it in the great single combat against his foster-brother Ferdiad in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Its name, often translated 'hard lightning' or 'hard cleft', describes a sword of fearsome cutting power. The word is the Irish cognate of the British Caledfwlch, the sword of Arthur better known as Excalibur, which makes Caladbolg the Irish link in the family of the great legendary blades of the Celtic world. In the tale of the Feast of Bricriu the sword is counted among the marvels tested by the heroes. No historical sword bearing the name survives, so its power is entirely in the literature, and it stands for the violent, glamorous world of the sagas.

name: Caduceus
powers: Symbolizes negotiation and safe passage; restores harmony.
description: The caduceus, the kērykeion, is the staff of the herald carried by Hermes, the messenger god, and in Greek literature it is the token of his office, the rod with which he conducts souls to the underworld, lulls the watchful, and opens the way before him; in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the staff is given to the young god by Apollo together with the golden wand and the arts of prophecy. Its familiar form, a staff entwined by two serpents and topped with a pair of wings, is the later iconography that became standard in Roman art and was revived in the Renaissance, and through it the caduceus came to stand for commerce, negotiation, and safe passage. The same image, easily confused with the single-serpent rod of the physician Asclepius, is now widely used as a medical symbol, though the two are distinct in origin. As the badge of the eloquent envoy, the caduceus remains the emblem of diplomacy itself.

name: Claíomh Mór
powers: Said to bite through any armor or shield.
description: Claíomh Mór, 'the great sword' of Irish tradition, is one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried with them when they came to Ireland, and later lore links it to Nuada Airgetlám, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn the sword of Nuada is said to be irresistible once drawn from its sheath, and it is listed beside the spear of Lugh, the cauldron of the Dagda and the stone of Fal. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light, a term that later folklore attached to the magic weapons of heroes and even to a buried golden sword that would rise against the invader. Some regional retellings describe the blade as drawing light from the Otherworld so that it blazed like a torch in battle. The sword remains a staple of Irish storytelling and has been invoked in poetry, ballad and political symbolism.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh ring, a gold or silver finger-ring shaped as two hands clasping a crowned heart, has been made in Galway since the seventeenth century and is named after the old fishing village of Claddagh beside the city. The design descends from the medieval 'fede' ring, whose clasped hands stood for faith and betrothal, with the heart and crown added locally. The best-known origin story tells of Richard Joyce, a Galway goldsmith who was captured by Algerian pirates in the late seventeenth century and sold into slavery in North Africa, where he supposedly made the ring before returning home; the tale is recorded in James Hardiman's 1820 History of Galway, though its details cannot be fully verified. The oldest surviving Claddagh ring, dated to about 1700 and stamped with Joyce's mark, is held by Galway City Museum. The ring is still a living custom, passed down from mother to daughter and worn in different positions to show whether the wearer is single or betrothed.

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, the Svatováclavská koruna, was made in 1347 for the coronation of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, and was named after the tenth-century Bohemian duke and martyr Saint Wenceslas. It is set with large rubies, sapphires, emeralds, spinels and pearls, and together with the orb, sceptre and coronation robes it forms the Bohemian crown jewels, now kept in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. The crown carries a famous curse: legend holds that a usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year, a fate sometimes connected with the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich, though the story is modern and unverifiable. Because of the legend the crown is shown rarely, displayed only on high feast days and under strict conditions, with seven keys held by separate officials. The medieval form, with its pointed arches and jewel-encrusted circlet, makes it one of the most striking royal insignia in Europe.

name: Cormac's Cup
powers: Shattered at a spoken lie and restored itself when truth was told.
description: The cup of Cormac mac Airt appears in Echtra Cormaic, the Adventure of Cormac, a medieval Irish tale in which a warrior who is really Manannán mac Lir gives the high king a golden cup in exchange for his wife and daughter. The cup is a cup of truth: if three lies are spoken over it, it breaks into pieces, and if three truths are told it is made whole again, so that Cormac uses it to test the words of his court. In the end Cormac learns that his wife and daughter have been carried to the Otherworld, and the cup is restored to him along with the lesson that no man can hold the truth's secrets without giving up what he loves. The tale, recorded in the Book of Ballymote and related manuscripts, belongs to the tradition of moral test-objects in Irish wonder literature. The cup is sometimes called the cup of truth, and its shattering and mending remain its best-known feature.
source: Echtra Cormaic (The Adventure of Cormac mac Airt)

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
powers: Brewed the Awen, the drops of inspiration and knowledge, for a year and a day.
description: Ceridwen's cauldron belongs to the medieval Ystoria Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin, in which the enchantress Ceridwen, a figure of wisdom and magic, brews a potion of inspiration and knowledge in a great cauldron for her son Afagddu. The brew must simmer for a year and a day, and the three drops of its divine inspiration, the Awen, fall instead on the boy Gwion, who guards the pot and swallows them, gaining all its wisdom at a stroke. Ceridwen pursues Gwion through a series of transformations, each side changing shape until she swallows him as a grain of wheat, and in time bears the child who becomes the poet Taliesin. The cauldron thus stands at the origin of the Welsh bardic tradition, the source of the Awen that inspires poets and seers. It is sometimes linked by scholars to the cauldrons of rebirth and plenty in Celtic myth. The object is wholly legendary, known only from the medieval tale and its retellings.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
powers: Fitted only Cinderella, letting the prince find her after the ball.
description: The glass slipper of Cinderella is the shoe lost as the heroine flees the prince's ball, the object that lets the prince find his bride because it fits no other foot in the kingdom. In the Grimms' version, Aschenputtel, the lost shoes are of gold, and the slipper motif belongs to the older tale-type in which the hero proves identity by an object that fits only the true owner. It was Charles Perrault's 1697 version, with its shoe of glass, that fixed the slipper in popular imagination, and the fragility of glass made it a perfect emblem of the tale's magic and brevity. Folklorists note that shoe-matching scenes occur in versions of the tale from China, where the heroine loses a shoe, to Europe, making it one of the oldest plot devices in storytelling. The glass slipper appears in no surviving material object, and no such slipper exists. It remains, with the pumpkin coach, the defining image of the Cinderella story.
source: Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen no. 21; Perrault

name: The Crook and Flail
aliases: Shepherd's Crook and Flail of Osiris
material: Gold and blue faience (mythic and royal)
powers: Signs of kingship and of Osiris's shepherd-care over the people.
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies in their coffins. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt and blue-faience examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun, whose tomb yielded several full sets. The crook descends from the shepherd's staff and the flail from the winnowing fan or cattle prod, and together they fix the enthroned image of Osiris that endured for three thousand years. In the Osiris myth the two signs, held by the dead god, tie the promise of the afterlife to the order of kingship that the pharaoh upheld on earth.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
powers: Reveals the whole world to the one who looks into it.
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing on earth or in the seven climes was hidden from the king, who used it in divination. Despite a common modern assumption, the cup does not appear in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh; it belongs to later literature, where it is also given to the Kayanid king Kay Khosrow, and it became a byword for far-seeing wisdom in the verses of Hafez and Attar. In later elaborations the cup was said to hold an elixir of immortality and to carry the seven rings of the heavens, and some described it as the 'cup of the seven planets' used like an astrolabe. Sufi poets read it as the purified heart that perceives divine truth, and in the twentieth century Allama Iqbal made it an image of the self that cannot be known from outside. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory, the xvaranah, are debated by scholars.

name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The cheonbuin, the heavenly seal, is the seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. In the Dangun foundation myth Hwanung established a sacred city at the summit, legislated for the people, and accepted the prayers of a bear and a tiger who wished to become human; the bear that endured the ordeal of a hundred days in a cave became the woman Ungnyeo, whose son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon. The seal is given to the king's descendants as the mark of royal mandate, anchoring Korean sovereignty in the descent of the royal line from heaven. The story is recorded in the Samguk Yusa and the Jewang Ungi, and it is the foundational myth of Korean identity, celebrated in the founding day festival of Gaecheonjeol. The cheonbuin is often paired in royal regalia with the sword of office, and the image of Hwanung descending with the seal is a fixed scene in Korean national symbolism.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
powers: Each shot could slay thousands
description: The magic crossbow of Co Loa is the weapon of An Duong Vuong, the legendary king of the Au Lac kingdom, whose trigger was forged from the golden claw of Kim Qui, the golden turtle god, and which could kill thousands of men with a single shot. The king built the spiral citadel of Co Loa with the turtle's help, but his defence was undone by his own daughter: My Chau, newly married to the spy Trong Thuy of the northern enemy, showed him the secret of the trigger, and the enemy stole it, the citadel fell, and An Duong Vuong fled with his daughter. Learning of the betrayal, the king beheaded My Chau, and her blood is said to have turned into pearls. The story is told in the Lĩnh Nam chích quái and the Dai Viet su ky toan thu, and it is one of the foundational legends of Vietnamese national memory, the site at Co Loa near Hanoi being among the oldest archaeological monuments of the country.

name: Cuauhxicalli
powers: Receptacle of sacrificial offerings at the temple.
description: A cuauhxicalli (Nahuatl 'eagle gourd bowl', from cuauhtli 'eagle' and xicalli 'gourd vessel') is a stone bowl that held the hearts of sacrificial victims in Aztec Tenochtitlan, placed before temple platforms where priests raised the still-beating heart to the sun before casting it into the vessel. Carvers shaped many examples as crouching eagles or jaguars with the bowl hollowed from the back; a celebrated andesite eagle cuauhxicalli found in the Templo Mayor precinct in 1985 measures some 139 centimetres. Others carry a sun disk carved inside and the earth goddess Tlaltecuhtli on the base, leading scholars such as Karl Taube to read the vessel as the earth's blood-filled womb receiving the sacrifice that renews the sun. The relief-covered Stone of Tizoc is sometimes identified as such a vessel, while the term also covers the reclining chacmool form that catches offerings on its belly. Spanish chroniclers and the colonial codices confirm the vessels' place at the centre of Mexica public ceremony.

name: Chac Mool
powers: Receives offerings to the gods at the temple.
description: A chac mool is a reclining stone figure with its head turned to one side, knees drawn up and a flat basin held on its stomach, set at the entrances of temples across Mesoamerica from Toltec Tula to Aztec Tenochtitlan and Maya Chichen Itza. The basin served as a receptacle for offerings, and in Aztec contexts the figure is especially linked to the rain god Tlaloc and to the hearts and blood of sacrifice. The name was coined in 1875 by the explorer Augustus Le Plongeon, who found one at Chichen Itza and dubbed it 'chac mool' from Maya terms, so it is a modern label for figures whose original name is unknown. Famous examples include the Temple of the Warriors chac mool and several recovered from the Templo Mayor of Mexico City. The form appears to have spread with the Toltec-influenced art of the Early Postclassic, and modern replicas have made the reclining figure one of the most familiar images of ancient Mexico.
source: Augustus Le Plongeon and later excavations at Tula and Tenochtitlan

name: Comal
era: From the classic era to the present
powers: Toasts tortillas and maize cakes over the hearth.
description: The comal is a flat, round clay griddle set on three hearth stones and used to toast tortillas, roast seeds and warm tamales across Mexico and Guatemala. The word comes from Nahuatl comalli, and clay comales appear in Mesoamerican archaeological sites from the Classic period onward, showing the griddle's deep roots in the region's cooking. Colonial accounts describe the round hearth as the fixed centre of the household kitchen, the comal standing always over the fire beside the metate where maize was ground. Potters still shape comales by hand, and the clay version is prized because it gives tortillas a particular toasted flavour, though metal comales have become common. In the mythology of everyday Mesoamerican life the comal completes the arc from maize harvest to tortilla, and it remains a standard tool of the Mexican and Central American kitchen.

name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
material: Stone bowl and wood stem, sometimes catlinite
powers: Binds treaties, prayers and peace in a single sacred act.
description: The calumet, or chanunpa in Lakota, is the sacred pipe of Plains peoples, a stone bowl joined to a wooden stem, smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace. In Lakota tradition the chanunpa was given to the people by White Buffalo Calf Woman, who taught its songs and the meaning of its smoke as a bridge between humans and the sacred. The word 'calumet' came from French traders by way of a Norman term for a reed pipe, reflecting how early Europeans witnessed its power to seal alliances. Catlinite, the red pipestone of southwestern Minnesota, was traded widely for the finest bowls. A pipe was a living sacred object: its keeper followed strict rules, and to smoke together bound the parties to truth, as the famous peace-pipe ceremonies with colonial powers recorded. The pipe remains central to Lakota ceremony and has become a lasting symbol of Indigenous diplomacy.
source: Lakota oral tradition and early French accounts

name: Cedar Bark Basket
culture: Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast peoples
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Holds water itself when woven tight enough.
description: Northwest Coast weavers, above all Haida, Tlingit and Tsimshian women, weave baskets and hats from shredded cedar bark and split cedar root, some so tightly that they hold water and can be used for cooking by dropping hot stones into the liquid. The twined technique, in which wefts are twisted around warp strands, produces the fine diagonal patterns that distinguish each nation's basketry, from simple checkerwork to complex animal and mountain designs. Cedar itself is honoured as a giver: in Haida tradition the cedar tree appears as Ts'uu Jaas, the Cedar Woman, a supernatural being whose generosity gave people the bark, wood and root for their tools and homes. Weavers harvest the inner bark in spring with prayers and care, taking only what the tree can spare. The art continues, and master weavers' baskets are now sought after by museums and collectors.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and ethnographic collections

name: Coup Stick
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow and others)
powers: Touching the enemy is the highest act of bravery.
description: The coup stick, or counting-coup staff, is a decorated staff or lance carried by Plains warriors such as the Lakota, Cheyenne and Crow for the act of 'counting coup', touching an enemy in battle without killing him. Among the Plains peoples touching a living enemy was ranked the bravest feat of war, above killing, and each time a warrior counted coup he added an honour, often marked on the staff with an eagle feather. The four grades of war honour were carefully ranked, and a man could also count coup on enemies' horses or possessions. Such sticks were wrapped with cloth and fur, hung with feathers, and treated with the respect due a record of personal bravery. Ethnographers recorded how these honours were proclaimed at dances, and the staff became the physical tally of a warrior's reputation.

name: Lechuguilla Mask
powers: Worn at the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes to escape King Herod.
description: The lechuguilla is the masked costume of the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes in Hatillo, Puerto Rico, held every December 28, when costumed runners race through the streets of the town in painted wire-mesh masks and gowns covered in ruffled fabric curls. The celebration descends from a custom brought by the Canary Island settlers who founded Hatillo in 1823, and it re-enacts the biblical Massacre of the Innocents: the masked runners, called corredores, take the part of King Herod's soldiers, hunting the Christ child, while the crowd flees and turns the hunt into a chase of laughter. The masks, made of cedazo wire covered in papier-mâché and painted in bright colors, are the work of local artisans, and the whole costume is often finished with a crown of fabric flowers or ribbons. Though the name lechuguilla is only partly explained, in Puerto Rico the same word names an aquatic plant, the festival itself is one of the island's most beloved traditions, a December carnival that has run for two centuries.

name: Chiwara Headdress
description: The chiwara is the antelope headdress of the Bamana of Mali, a carved figure with a long neck, elegant horns and an openwork body, danced in pairs at the agricultural festivals in honor of the mythic being who, the Bamana say, taught humanity to farm. The dance re-enacts the teaching: the headdresses are tied to a cap on the heads of two dancers who leap and crouch like antelopes feeding, while the rest of the village raises the hoe to the rhythm. The long horns curve toward the sun, and the zigzag crest on the back of the older style recalls the sun's rays falling on the fields; two forms are recognized, the vertical style of the north and the horizontal style of the south. The chiwara is not worshiped but honored, it is the remembered teacher of agriculture, and the dance gives thanks for the gift. Today the headdress is among the best-known of African sculptures, though it is still danced at sowing time in the Bamana villages.

name: Chokwe Pwo Mask
material: Carved wood, pigment, fibre and feathers
description: The pwo is the carved female mask of the Chokwe of Angola and neighbouring lands, with a finely finished face, gently closed eyes, and filed or scarified markings on the forehead and cheeks. Danced at the mukanda initiations that turn boys into men and at celebrations of the community, the mask embodies the idealised ancestress, Mwana Pwo, the Young Woman, whose beauty and calm set the standard of Chokwe womanhood. The dancer who wears it takes on the gentle, swaying movements of a woman, while a headdress of fibre and feathers completes the costume. Pwo masks come in pairs with the male cihongo mask of the chief, and both are danced with wit and prestige. Carvers claim to receive guidance in dreams, and each mask is finished with a dark patina meant to evoke the oiled skin of a beautiful woman. Chokwe carving, of which the pwo is the best-known face, has been admired since the first pieces reached Europe.

name: Chokwe Chief's Throne
description: The carved wooden thrones of the Chokwe chiefs of Angola are low seats supported by figural groups, ancestors, rulers, hunters, and scenes of everyday life, that turn each throne into a small chronicle of the chiefdom. The seat and backrest are often studded with brass tacks and worked with openwork motifs, while the supporting figures served as personal emblems of the soba and his lineage. Thrones were made by the chief's carvers and passed down the chiefly line, and a new ruler might commission a throne that linked him to the ancestors shown beneath the seat. In Chokwe court culture the throne was a public statement of the dignity of the soba and the continuity of power, used at audiences and ceremonies. The same woodcarvers made the masks, drums, and staffs of office that completed chiefly regalia. Museum examples from the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries have made the Chokwe throne a celebrated form of Central African royal art.

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a mouth bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden stave with a single fibre or wire string, held against the open mouth and plucked so that the mouth shapes the tone. Because the cavity of the mouth acts as a resonator, the player can vary pitch and timbre while the string keeps up a light, rhythmic pattern. It is above all an instrument of herders and young men, who play it alone in the fields to pass the hours, to court, and to accompany themselves while singing. The chipendani is small and portable, carried in the hand or tucked in the belt, and its soft sound suits the quiet company of cattle rather than the crowd. Related mouth bows appear across southern Africa under different names. Although the mbira overshadowed it in the modern Shona music revival, the chipendani is still heard in the countryside and is taught in some schools and cultural programmes.

name: Chaoui Aures Kilim
description: The Chaoui kilim is a flat-woven woollen rug made by the Chaoui Amazigh women of the Aures mountains in eastern Algeria. Because the Aures is a cold, high country of oak forests and steppe, the weavers use the fleece of the local sheep to create blankets, saddle cloths, tent curtains and floor rugs, working on a horizontal ground loom that can be set up and dismantled as families move between seasonal pastures. The weaving is warp-faced, so that the geometric design is visible on both faces, and the patterns of diamonds, ladders, zigzags and small protective 'eye' motifs are handed down within each family rather than copied from books. Dyes traditionally came from madder roots, walnut husks, indigo and other plants gathered in the mountains, giving a palette of warm reds, browns and indigo against undyed cream wool. Like other Amazigh textiles, the Aures kilim carried apotropaic meaning, with border motifs believed to turn aside the evil eye, and today these rugs are also valued by collectors as documents of Chaoui identity.
source: Studies of Amazigh weaving (e.g. Ianthe Reswick)

name: Canopic Jar
era: Ancient Egyptian (Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic era)
description: Canopic jars are the four vessels in which ancient Egyptian embalmers placed the organs removed from the body during mummification, the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines being preserved separately so that the deceased could use them again in the afterlife. The jars, made of alabaster, limestone, wood or pottery, stood in the tomb chest beside the coffin, and by late times each lid was carved as the head of one of the Four Sons of Horus, the protective genii Imsety, Hapy, Duamutef and Qebehsenuef. Spell 151 of the Book of the Dead invokes these guardians, and the whole procedure was overseen by Anubis, the jackal-headed god of embalming who is said to have invented mummification when he treated the body of Osiris. The practice of preserving the viscera is attested from the Old Kingdom onward and illustrates the Egyptians' conviction that the body must remain intact for the next life. Excavated canopic sets, with their carved lids and painted texts, are among the most recognizable objects of the Egyptian burial assemblage.
source: Ancient Egyptian funerary archaeology; museum collections

name: Coolamon
description: The coolamon is the carved wooden carrying dish of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, shaped from the root growth of eucalyptus trees or cut from bark, and used to hold water, food, seeds, fire and babies. A single piece of wood is gouged and shaped so that the dish has a curved bottom, and it is carried on the head, in the hand or under the arm, with smaller coolamons made as cradles for infants and larger ones used for grinding seeds and winnowing grain. The dish is a working tool of daily life, used especially by women in food gathering, and it can be painted with the clan designs of the maker. In the desert and riverine regions the coolamon remains a practical and ceremonial vessel, and examples are held in museum collections of Aboriginal material culture.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of the riverine and desert peoples
source: Museum and ethnographic records of Aboriginal material culture

name: Clapsticks
description: The clapsticks are the paired hardwood percussion sticks of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, struck together by singers and dancers to mark the rhythm of ceremony and song. In Arnhem Land they are known as bilma, and they are often painted or engraved with the designs of the clan, with the length and tone of each pair chosen by the songman. The sticks accompany the didgeridoo and the singing in corroboree and ceremony, and each song owns a particular beat that encodes the Dreaming story it carries, so the rhythm is part of the knowledge held by the singers. Clapsticks are simple in form but exact in use, and they are also played by hand-clapping groups where no wood is at hand, in the musical traditions of the north and the centre of Australia.
maker: Aboriginal craftsmen of Arnhem Land and the north

name: Cook Islands Adze (Toki)
description: Stone-bladed adze of the Cook Islands, ground from fine-grained basalt and lashed to a wooden handle with sennit, used to fell and shape the timber for canoes, houses, war clubs and carvings. The toki was the essential tool of the master craftsman, and the quarries that supplied the prized basalt — above all the great quarry on Mangaia — were controlled by chiefly families and treated as resources of mana. Fine adzes were treasured heirlooms, their lashing and finish a mark of the carver's standing, and the same tool type, its design carried by voyagers across the Pacific, appears in the founding histories of many island traditions.
material: basalt stone, wooden handle, fibre lashing
source: Archaeological and ethnographic records of Cook Islands technology

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted baubles made in the glass towns of northern Bohemia, above all around Jablonec nad Nisou and the Krkonoše foothills, where the craft grew out of the region's bead and glass-button industry in the mid-nineteenth century. Workers blew thin globes from molten glass, silvered them from inside with a solution that gave the characteristic metallic glimmer, and then painted them by hand with snow, berries, flowers or fairy-tale figures before hanging them from the family fir tree. The delicate ornaments became a celebrated export, so prized that Bohemian and Moravian glassmakers supplied Christmas trees across Europe and America for more than a century. A few family workshops still fire the baubles by mouth today, and the region's museums display both the finished ornaments and the wooden and metal tools of the old glasshuts.

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the decorated shepherd's cloak of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length mantle of white felt cut from a single piece, split down the middle so the wearer can slip it over the shoulders and pin it under the chin. Its name pairs szűr, the plain cloak of Hungarian herdsmen, with cifra, 'ornamented', and indeed the best cifraszűr covers the felt with black, red and green wool applique arranged in rosettes, tulips, fringes and braided borders. Herdsmen wore the szűr against sun and rain and slept in it on the puszta, and a richly worked cloak was a sign of skill, wealth and pride, passed down in the family or given as a groom's gift. By the twentieth century the cifraszűr had moved from pasture to festival dress and museum collections, remaining a striking emblem of Hungarian shepherd culture.
material: white wool felt, coloured wool thread

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary, identified with the crown of the first king Saint Stephen I (ruled 1000-1038), is a circlet of gold hung with enamelled plaques, pearls and gemstones, with a distinctive cross set at an angle on top. Scholars date the surviving bands and figures to the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the crown as it exists today was almost certainly assembled from older parts for later coronations, so its precise age and original form are still debated. It was used to crown Hungarian kings from the Middle Ages down to Charles IV in 1916, the last Hungarian coronation, and legend held that no ruler who wore it could ever be overthrown. Hidden in chests, walled into castles and smuggled abroad over the centuries, the crown returned to Hungary from the United States in 1978 and has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building since 2000 as the supreme symbol of Hungarian statehood.
aliases: Crown of Saint Stephen of Hungary
source: Academic studies of the Hungarian coronation insignia

name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: The chokha is the traditional men's coat of the Caucasus, a long woollen garment with a fitted waist, a flared skirt and, most distinctively, rows of small cartridge cases - the gazyr - sewn diagonally across the chest. The gazyr began as real ammunition holders, with silver, wood or bone caps, and survived as ornament long after firearms made them obsolete, so the decorated chest became the emblem of Caucasian dress. In Georgia the chokha has been worn since at least the seventeenth century, with regional cuts: the Khevsur highland variant is richly embroidered in wool, while the plain dark chokha of the lowlands is the classic civic and military coat. After generations of everyday use the chokha is today reserved for festivals, folk dance, weddings and ceremonial occasions, and it remains the strongest single emblem of Georgian national dress.
source: Georgian National Museum, Tbilisi; ethnographic dress studies of the Caucasus

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: The chonguri is the four-string fretless lute of western Georgia, carved from a single block of walnut or maple into a shallow bowl, with a flat spruce soundboard and a short drone string called the zili that buzzes beneath the melody strings. It is the instrument of Guria and Samegrelo, where it traditionally accompanied women's songs and the nadi, the evening working gatherings at which women spun, wove and sang, and where the chonguri's quiet, flexible tone fitted a female voice. Unlike the fretted panduri of the east, the chonguri is played with a light, flowing touch, and its three melody strings are named after the three voices of Georgian polyphony. Still made and taught today, the chonguri belongs to the living polyphonic tradition that UNESCO inscribed in 2008.
material: walnut or maple, spruce soundboard, nylon strings
source: Smithsonian 'Georgian Chonguri' object of the day; Georgian folk instrument studies (Arakishvili)

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: The chuniri is the bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, a round or tubular wooden body with a skin soundboard, three gut or horsehair strings and a heavy bow, held against the shoulder like a small violin. Because a bowed string can sustain a note, the chuniri is said to sing in place of a human voice, standing in for a singer in Svan hunting songs, work songs and choral polyphony; its two-string cousin, the chianuri, serves the same role in other highland regions such as Racha and Adjara. The instrument was the personal companion of Svan shepherds and hunters, who played it at home, at vigils and in the towers of the mountain villages. It remains one of the two bowed instruments of Georgia, heard at festivals and in the polyphonic ensembles that carry Svan tradition.
material: wood body, skin soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Wikipedia 'Chuniri'; Georgian folk music instrument documentation

name: Cimbalom (Hungarian Hammered Dulcimer)
description: Large hammered dulcimer of Hungary, a trapezoid box with rows of metal strings struck by small wooden hammers; the concert cimbalom developed in Budapest in the 1870s. It appears in Romani music and in the works of composers such as Kodály and Bartók, while its village relatives are played across Eastern Europe; the Hungarian word cimbalom names the whole family of hammered dulcimers. The instrument has two registers of strings crossing the soundboard, a damping pedal to stop the ringing, and a boxy, resonant tone that carries clearly in a hall. Virtuoso players command a solo repertoire, and the cimbalom is also used in gypsy bands, where it once set the tempo and the harmony. Since the 19th century it has travelled to the Americas with emigrants, and it remains a fixture of Hungarian folk and folk-influenced classical music.
material: wood box, metal strings, wooden hammers
era: concert form from the 1870s; village instruments older
source: Hungarian cimbalom tradition; Kodály and Bartók repertoire

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture. Its head resembles an ice-axe, with a short blade on one side and a rounded butt on the other, and it serves as a climbing stick, a lever, and a defence against wolves and bears. The wooden haft, up to a metre long, is a canvas for ornament: stars, suns and geometric bands are burned or incised into the ash or beech wood. The zbójnicki, the dance of the historic brigands who sheltered in the mountains, is performed with the ciupaga raised and struck, and the object remains a proud mark of highland identity worn on formal dress.
material: steel blade, ash or beech haft
source: Podhale highland culture studies; Tatra Museum, Zakopane

name: Choron (Yakut Kumys Vessel)
description: Carved wooden drinking vessel of the Yakut (Sakha) people, made from a single piece of birch or spruce burl, with a conical or rounded body and short legs. The choron is the principal ritual vessel of the ysyakh summer festival, filled with kumys and offered in honour of the aiyy deities, then shared among the celebrants; its elegant form is held to resemble a bird. The body swells gently from a small mouth and stands on three or four short carved legs, and the outer surface is often engraved with bands of geometric ornament. At the festival the first choron of kumys is raised to the sky and poured to the four directions, and the celebrants then drink in turn, some vessels holding several litres. The carving follows the grain of the burl, and the best chorons are so carefully balanced that they stand firm on uneven ground. Old examples in Sakha museums show the same proportions as those made today, the form passed down unchanged for centuries.

name: Yaranga (Chukchi Portable Dwelling)
description: Large hemispherical tent dwelling of the coastal Chukchi, built on a wooden frame of poles and whale ribs and covered with walrus skins, with reindeer hides laid inside against the cold. A family camp could stretch up to twenty metres; inside, fur-lined sleeping chambers formed separate rooms. The yaranga was central to Chukchi coastal life. Its frame is assembled from long poles set in a circle and tied at the top, with heavy walrus hides laid over the sides and secured against the wind with stones and lines; the interior is divided into a cold outer ring and a warm inner chamber, the polog, a tent of reindeer hides where the family sleeps. Reindeer-herding Chukchi carried lighter versions that could be packed on sleds and pitched in an hour, while the coastal people built the heavier skin yarangas of the sea-hunters. The yaranga is sometimes said to turn its entrance away from the wind, and travellers could enter it even without invitation. Skins and poles are still used in Chukotka today.
material: wooden poles, whale ribs, walrus skins, reindeer hides

name: Chukchi Walrus-Ivory Carving
description: Carved objects of the Chukchi and Siberian Yupik of the Chukotka coast, worked from walrus tusks into harpoon heads, amulets, figurines and engraved scenes of sea-hunting and animal life. Walrus ivory carving is a hallmark of Chukchi art, celebrated by the Uelen bone-carving workshop and collected by the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The tusk is cut and sawn, then shaped with knives and polished with the hide of the walrus itself, and engravers trace outlines of hunters, walruses, whales and spirits in fine, firm lines. In the past ivory was also the material of daily life: harpoon points, toggles and needle cases were carved for use at sea, and small figurines were carried as charms. The workshop at Uelen, founded in the 1930s on the Bering coast, gathered carvers of the Chukchi and Yupik villages and gave the craft a lasting home. Ivory is sometimes said to hold the luck of the hunt, and a well-carved tusk remains a family treasure on the Chukotka coast.
maker: Chukchi and Siberian Yupik carvers, including the Uelen workshop
source: Wikipedia 'Walrus ivory carving'; ar.culture.ru Chukotka collections
